steps.explanationAfterStep: Protonation makes the carbonyl group a much stronger electron sink, ready for enolisation.
This is the slow step. The rate depends on the ketone and the acid but not on bromine: chlorine, bromine and iodine all react at the same rate, the rate of enolisation.
The enol attacks bromine like an alkene, but the oxygen lone pair makes it far more nucleophilic and the cation formed is a stable protonated ketone, not a bromonium ion.

The acid is given back and HBr is formed, so the reaction makes its own catalyst. It stops after one bromine: bromine on the α-carbon makes the carbonyl oxygen less basic, so the next enolisation is slower.

title: Acid-catalysed bromination of acetone
subtitle: The enol attacks bromine
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 20

enol.caption: the enol + H₃O⁺ + water + bromine
hintTiers: An enol is an electron-rich alkene: the oxygen lone pair pushes electrons into the C=C bond. Which carbon is nucleophilic?
The oxygen lone pair forms C=O⁺, the C=C π electrons attack a bromine atom, and the Br–Br bond breaks onto the other bromine. Three arrows.
Enol oxygen lone pair → a π bond to its carbon; the C=C π bond → a new bond from the CH₂ carbon to bromine; the Br–Br bond → a lone pair on the far bromine.
enol.learnerPrompt: The enol is the nucleophile. Attack bromine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: An O–Br bond is weak and gains nothing. The enol reacts at carbon: the oxygen lone pair pushes, the C=C π bond attacks.
Protonating the enol on carbon gives back the protonated ketone. Bromine is the electrophile here.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right bonds, but this leaves a carbocation next to the OH. Push the oxygen lone pair in too, to form C=O⁺–H.

reactants.caption: acetone + H₃O⁺ + water + bromine (Br⁻ is a spectator)
hintTiers: Bromine needs a nucleophile, and acetone is not one. Acid catalysis turns the ketone into a nucleophile, the enol. What is its first step?
The carbonyl oxygen takes a proton from H₃O⁺. Two arrows.
Carbonyl oxygen lone pair → the hydrogen of H₃O⁺; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the oxygen of H₃O⁺.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Bromine does not react with the ketone itself. Start by protonating the ketone.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: A ketone is not nucleophilic enough to attack bromine. First make the enol: protonate the carbonyl oxygen.
The α-hydrogen of the neutral ketone is not acidic enough for water. Protonate the carbonyl oxygen first.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right start: the carbonyl oxygen takes the proton. Now break the hydrogen's bond to the oxygen of H₃O⁺.

protonated-ketone.caption: protonated acetone + water + bromine
hintTiers: The protonated carbonyl makes the α-C–H acidic. Which C–H is drawn?
Water takes the drawn α-hydrogen; the C–H electrons form a C=C bond; the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Water lone pair → the drawn α-hydrogen; that C–H bond → a π bond to the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π bond → a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.
protonated-ketone.learnerPrompt: Form the enol, using water as the base.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Water can add to the carbonyl carbon, but the hydrate is a reversible dead end. Water acts as a base here.
Nothing here is nucleophilic enough for bromine yet. Make the enol first: water removes an α-hydrogen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the C=C forms. The carbonyl carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π electrons onto oxygen.

protonated-bromoketone.caption: protonated bromoacetone + bromide + H₃O⁺ + water
hintTiers: The product still carries a proton on its carbonyl oxygen. Which species can take it?
A water molecule takes the proton on oxygen. Two arrows.
Water lone pair → the hydrogen on the carbonyl oxygen; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.
protonated-bromoketone.learnerPrompt: Deprotonate the oxygen to give the neutral product.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Bromide can add to the carbonyl carbon, but that falls apart again. Remove the proton from the oxygen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: water takes the proton. Now break the O–H bond onto the carbonyl oxygen.

mechanismSummary: Acid protonates the ketone, water removes an α-proton to give the enol, and the enol's C=C π bond attacks bromine while the oxygen lone pair forms C=O⁺–H. Water then removes that proton. Enol formation is the slow step, so the rate does not depend on the halogen. In acid the reaction stops after one halogen; in base it does not (the haloform reaction).
